stories.title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
stories.summary: ShipStation Global's engineering team built Deckhand, an AI IT help desk agent for Slack on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers routine IT questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and files Jira tickets. In its first three months it resolved 97.5% of channel queries with a 96% positive feedback rating.

sources.title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Banh, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global. Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand , an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets. In this post, we discuss how ShipStation architected Deckhand, which resulted in resolving 97.5 percent of incoming channel queries while earning a 96 percent positive feedback rating by employees (Figure 1). Figure 1: 3-month channel coverage and positive feedback The problem Deckhand solves is the one every IT team will recognize: the same questions are routinely asked, error messages are posted after business hours, and information needs to be gathered from different teams. At ShipStation Global, those conversations lived in a busy help desk Slack channel, where employees asked, and IT answered, one thread at a time. The answers usually already existed in a Confluence how-to article, on a company intranet page, or in a thread from eight months earlier. Finding them was the hard part. The channel data made the scale concrete. In the 12 months before launch: “We created Deckhand because getting help should be as simple as asking a question in Slack, not deciphering a ticket form or sending an email into the void. We believe that tickets are an indication of operational friction not productivity. Deckhand resolves common questions on the spot and, when it can’t, converts the conversation into a fully contextualized ticket with one click, improving the employee experience and freeing our team from endlessly repeating the phrase: ‘Please file a ticket.’” — Chris Collins, Senior Director IT at ShipStation Global Deckhand works in Slack like any teammate—joining channels, reading the conversation, and drawing context from Slack profiles to answer IT questions in place. We run it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, hosts the agent in isolated sessions, so we run no servers or containers. The solution has four main components, shown in Figure 2: Figure 2: Architecture diagram showing Slack events entering the Slack service and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, with separate paths to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, AgentCore Gateway-backed Lambda tools, Jira Service Management, and DynamoDB feedback. When an employee posts in a channel where Deckhand is a member, the Slack service assembles the full thread history and user context. It then invokes the agent through the AgentCore runtime API. The agent searches the knowledge base and calls tools as needed. When it finds an answer, it returns a final response (Figure 3). When it doesn’t, it asks a clarifying question or offers to create a ticket (Figure 4). Figure 3: Deckhand responds with self-service steps Figure 4: Deckhand offers to create a ticket This section walks through how Deckhand is implemented, from prerequisites to a working deployment. To implement this pattern, you need the following: The agent is intentionally lightweight. Using the open source Strands Agents SDK , an agent consists of a model, a set of tools, and a system prompt. The SDK manages the reasoning loop, allowing the model to select tools, process results, and iterate until it produces an answer. Deckhand’s agent service is implemented in a few lines of Python. The model ID is set through an environment variable, which allows switching models without modifying application code. Tools are integrated with the agent in two ways. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval is a native Strands tool that supports knowledge base search with a single import. Other functions, including classification, ticket management, user resolution, and image analysis, are handled by a Lambda function registered on AgentCore Gateway. The Gateway exposes these as MCP tools, and the Lambda routes each invocation by tool name. This separation allows tool logic to be updated independently, and the agent can access new tools from the Gateway without requiring a rebuild. AgentCore runtime hosts the agent as a container, avoiding the need for server or session management. The Slack service calls the agent synchronously for each message, providing the thread transcript and user context, and posts the final response. Since context, including the employee’s profile, is included with every request, the agent can complete ticket details automatically. Deckhand answers from a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with core S3-backed data sources: Each document includes metadata such as title, source URL, content type, and event dates. This allows the agent to filter content, for example, when users ask about upcoming events or weekly lunch menus in the Austin office. The most valuable data source is the archive of resolved support threads. Before Deckhand existed, Slack was where problems got solved: years of employees describing issues and IT walking them through fixes. That history is an organic knowledge base, validated by the best possible reviewer: the person whose problem got fixed. It’s also noisy: a raw export mixes banter, automated alerts, and threads that never actually got resolved. sources.title: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology
sources.text: Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work. Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch Analyst-hours of investigation completed each quarter At Block, the company behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks. Block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a new teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, says. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.” Projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result. For example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming. The team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he says. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path. The automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely new autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim says, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.” Traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years. In one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy issue on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of issues. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James says. Another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes. Finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the issue lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.” While agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim says, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.” Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry. 18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises. Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back. Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter. 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations. Detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly. As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. sources.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
sources.text: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. stories.title: AI costs: what teams pay to use AI tools
stories.summary: AI costs explained: how AI tools are priced, what drives a team's bill, and how to compare plans by cost per task.

sources.name: Perplexity
sources.title: AI costs: what teams pay to use AI tools
sources.text: How AI tools are priced, what drives a team's bill, and how to compare plans by the work they get done. AI costs are what a team pays to use AI tools. They fall into three types: Take a hypothetical 10-person team paying $25 per person per month for an AI research tool. The subscription is a fixed $250. In busy months, two analysts run out of included credits and the team buys $100 more, so the bill runs to $350. Rollout adds 18 hours of staff time that never appears on an invoice: eight hours for an operations lead to connect the tool to the company's sign-in system, and an hour of training for each of the 10 team members. AI tools use seven main pricing models. Many plans combine two or more, such as a subscription with included credits. Grammarly's free plan includes a monthly allowance of AI prompts Testing whether a tool fits a team's work before paying for it GitHub Copilot Business is billed per user each month Teams where most people use the tool regularly and at similar levels Claude's Max plan offers 5 or 20 times the usage of its Pro plan People who regularly hit standard limits or run multi-step tasks Adobe's Creative Cloud plans include a monthly allocation of generative credits Teams whose heavy AI work comes in bursts, such as campaign launches Perplexity's Sonar API (for adding search-based answers to other apps) charges by length of questions and answers plus a flat fee per question Teams with technical staff building AI into their own products or workflows Microsoft 365 Copilot is an annual per-user enterprise add-on to Microsoft 365 Organizations that need security reviews and central administration Intercom's Fin charges per outcome, such as a resolved customer conversation High-volume work with a countable result, such as customer support Free plans charge nothing but cap how much each person can use the tool, and they usually leave out the most capable models and some features. When a person reaches the cap, the tool stops handling that type of request or switches to a less capable model until the limit resets. A seat is a license for one named user, and per-seat plans charge a set price for each seat, billed monthly or annually. Team versions usually add admin controls, such as deciding who has access. The bill scales with headcount rather than with use, so a person who runs two queries a week costs the same as one who runs 200. Premium tiers are higher-priced individual plans with higher usage limits, more capable models, or more advanced features. They're still priced per person, so a team pays the higher rate only for each person it upgrades. Credit plans include a monthly allowance that tasks use up at different rates. Usually complex tasks use more credits than simple ones. When the allowance runs out, people can wait for it to reset or buy more. Unused credits often expire. Credits usually sit on top of a subscription rather than replacing it. Teams that build AI into their own software or workflows pay through an API, which lets software send requests to an AI model directly. API usage is billed per token (small chunk of text). A short, common word is usually one token, while longer words are split into two or more. Both the text sent to the model and the text it generates count toward the bill. Some APIs add per-request fees on top. Enterprise plans combine seats with advanced security and administration features, such as single sign-on and controls over how long data is stored. Pricing is typically annual, and listed per seat or set by quote. Some enterprise AI plans are add-ons that require a separate base license, so their cost comes on top of software the company already pays for. Outcome-based pricing charges for a completed result rather than for access or usage, so the bill depends on how the vendor defines a result. Intercomâs Fin, for example, bills only once per customer conversation. Standard individual plans for the most widely used AI tools cost about $20 a month. Premium individual tiers run $100 to $500. Business seats cost about $14 to $40 per user per month. Business: $20 billed annually, $25 monthly $20 billed annually, plus usage at API rates Google Workspace Business Standard: $14 billed annually, $16.80 monthly Google Workspace Enterprise: custom quote Copilot Business: $18-$21 billed annually, plus a Microsoft 365 plan Microsoft 365 Copilot: $30 billed annually, plus a Microsoft 365 plan Prices in USD as of October 2026. Prices are subject to change. Check vendor websites for current pricing. Development teams may spend more on AI than other teams, because coding tools increasingly run agents. To take one example, Anthropic reports that Claude Code averages about $13 per developer per active day, or $150 to $250 per developer per month, across enterprise deployments. For comparison, a standard seat on Anthropic's business plan costs $20 per user per month, or roughly $1 per active day for someone who stays within the plan's included usage. Using Gemini pricing as an example, Gartner suggests budgeting by usage level : Agent workflows or high-volume automated tasks Take a hypothetical 10-person development team on a plan that charges $20 per seat plus usage. 6 developers using the tool on most working days 1 developer running coding agents most of the day This is a modest budget for a team using AI tools with restraint. If a developer uses frontier models 24/7 across multiple agents, costs can compound quickly. And as a developer team uses AI tools more aggressively, expect the costs to increase. Four factors shape what a team spends on AI tools: On seat-based plans, the bill depends on how many people need their own login, not on how many people benefit from the tool's output. A research lead might use an AI tool to produce a report that 10 colleagues read, but only the research lead will need a seat. Team plans often set a minimum number of seats, so a very small team can end up paying for more seats than it uses. Every step an AI t

sources.title: What Are MCP Tools and How Do AI Models Use Them?
sources.text: Learn what MCP tools are, how AI models find and call them through MCP servers, and how to use them safely. MCP tools are functions an AI model can call to perform a task outside the conversation. For example, search your notes or query a database. Each tool sits on an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server and has a name and a short description that help the model decide when to use it. The term "MCP tool" is used in other ways too. In everyday use, people say "MCP tools" when they mean MCP servers (the applications that offer tools) or the directories that list those servers. MCP Tools is also the name of a command-line program for listing and calling the tools on an MCP server. This guide is about the protocol functions, not servers, directories, or command lines. It explains what a tool consists of, the kinds of tools servers offer, and how tools differ from resources, prompts, and function calling. It then walks through the steps a model takes to use a tool, and closes with the most common problems related to their use. An MCP tool is a function that lets AI models complete tasks with other software applications. For instance, my AI agents and workflows use MCP tools to draft emails in Gmail ( create_draft ), create Trello cards ( trelloWriteCard ), and pull live search results from DataForSEO ( serp_organic_live_advanced ), to name just a few. Software apps often offer multiple MCP tools on their MCP servers. For example, the Trello MCP server currently has 14 MCP tools that enable AI models to read and update boards, lists, checklists, cards, and more. And because MCP standardizes how tools are described and offered, any AI app that supports the protocol can use the same MCP tool. Some tools add extra metadata: a display name, a description of the results they return (an output schema), and annotations about how the tool behaves. The AI model never sees the code behind a tool. It works from what the tool says about itself, so a vague name or description leads the model to pick the wrong tool. MCP tools fall into four groups by what they do: Besides MCP tools, an MCP server can offer two other types of building blocks, which the protocol calls primitives: resources and prompts. For example, GitHub's official MCP server offers: The difference is what each one does and who decides when to use one: you, the AI app you're working in (e.g., Perplexity), or the AI model running inside that app. An AI model uses an MCP tool in five steps: discovery, tool selection, invocation, results, and error handling. Your AI app passes everything between the model and the server. Say you ask your AI app to check your Trello "This week" list and draft an email to your editor with an update. Here's what happens end to end: The key point is that the model chooses tools from their descriptions alone, and your AI app does all the talking to servers. Problems with MCP tools come down to four things: how many tools are connected, how they're named and described, how much data they return, and which servers they come from. Here's what each problem looks like and what helps: Every tool definition sits in the model's context window before you've asked anything, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Connect only the servers a task needs, and turn off unused tools where your AI app allows it. Example: GitHub's MCP server lets you enable only the groups of tools (toolsets) you need. The model calls the wrong tool, or the right one with the wrong inputs, because two descriptions sound alike or one says too little. Provide clear, specific names and descriptions, ideally with an example of when to use the tool. If a server's tools keep misfiring, MCP Inspector, the official testing tool, shows exactly what each tool says about itself. Two servers each offer a tool called search , and there's no telling which one a call is meant for. Prefix tool names with the server's name. Example: Trello's server ( trelloSearch , trelloReadList ). A tool returns more than the task needs, such as a whole email thread with its formatting, and crowds the model's context. Use tools that offer compact formats. Example: Gmail's get_thread tool description recommends plain-text format "to prevent context exhaustion." A careless or malicious server could use tool calls to pull data out of your conversation. Connect servers only from sources you trust, and keep approvals on for tools that change things or send data out. MCP tools need your approval because, without it, the AI model could make changes you didn't intend or share sensitive data with a server you don't control. A misread request or a vaguely described tool can trigger the wrong action. Every call also sends some of your information to a server. That's why the protocol expects AI apps to keep a person in the loop, with the ability to deny any tool call. Here's a practical way to sort tools by how much checking they need: Perplexity works with MCP tools in both directions: it can use tools from MCP servers you connect, and it offers its own tools to other AI apps. No, MCP isn't just tool calling. Tool calling is how the model asks for a tool, and MCP is how the AI app finds tools and routes each call to the server that runs it. Tool calling (also called function calling) is the AI model's part of the job: the model sees a list of tools and replies with a request to run one. With tool calling alone, each AI app has to define and run every tool itself. MCP lets tools live on servers, so any AI app that supports MCP can offer them to its model and send the model's requests to the right server. No, MCP won't replace APIs, because MCP and APIs work together. MCP tools often sit on top of existing APIs, and when the model calls a tool, the MCP server typically makes an API request. sources.title: Mix, Don't Tune: Bilingual Pre-Training Outperforms Hyperparameter Search in Data-Constrained Settings
sources.text: Mix, Donât Tune: Bilingual Pre-Training Outperforms Hyperparameter Search in Data-Constrained Settings Authors Paul Jehaâ **, Anastasiia Sedova, Louis BÃ©thune, Skyler Seto, Jes Frellsenâ â¡, Pierre Ablinâ¡, Natalie Schluterâ¡ For most languages of the world, language model pre-training operates in a data-constrained regime where models must repeat their training data many times, degrading generalization. Two remedies exist: aggressive hyperparameter tuning such as high weight decay, and mixing in data from a high-resource auxiliary language to directly aid the low-resource target. While hyperparameter tuning regularizes the model by shrinking weights to restrict network capacity, auxiliary data mixing uses a tunable mixing ratio to expand the training distribution and diversify the training signal with new knowledge. Both offer a principled way to improve training in a data-constrained domain. We compare these levers systematically across four model scales from 150M to 1.43B parameters, using Arabic as the low-resource target and English as the auxiliary, over approximately 1000 pre-training runs. Three findings emerge. First, mixing yields larger improvements than hyperparameter tuning on both validation loss and downstream task accuracy, and the gap grows with model size. Second, we quantify how much mixing helps: it boosts performance by an amount equivalent to 2â3Ã the unique target data on validation loss and 2â13Ã on downstream task accuracy, with the gain scaling steeply with model size. Third, this divergence reveals that target-language validation loss systematically underestimates mixingâs value. Mixing regularizes by diversifying the training signal and contributes knowledge the repeated target corpus cannot supply; validation loss captures only the first effect. Our practical recommendations are: mix in a high-resource language, prioritize the mixing ratio over hyperparameter tuning, and transfer hyperparameters from a small proxy model via Î¼P. Completed Hyperparameter Transfer across Modules, Width, Depth, Batch and Duration February 13, 2026 research area Methods and Algorithms conference ICLR Hyperparameter tuning can dramatically impact training stability and final performance of large-scale models. Recent works on neural network parameterisations, such as Î¼P, have enabled transfer of optimal global hyperparameters across model sizes. These works propose an empirical practice of search for optimal global base hyperparameters at a small model size, and transfer to a large size. We extend these works in two key ways. To handle scalingâ¦ Scaling Laws for Forgetting During Finetuning with Pretraining Data Injection June 20, 2025 research area Methods and Algorithms conference ICML A widespread strategy for obtaining a language model that performs well in a target domain is to fine-tune it by training it to do unsupervised next-token prediction on data from that domain. Fine-tuning presents two challenges: i) if the amount of target data is limited, as is the case in most practical applications, the model will quickly overfit, and ii) the model will drift away from the original model and forget the pre-trainingâ¦ Our research in machine learning breaks new ground every day.
